blocks.text: Nomusa Makhubu on live art, cultural access and reimagining Cape Town through performance

Ahead of the Live Art Festival, ICA Director Professor Nomusa Makhubu speaks with ART AFRICA about the festival’s expansion across Cape Town, from the city centre to KwaLanga, and how live art can engage the city’s spatial histories, broaden cultural access, and create new encounters between art, place, and public life. Official Poster for the ICA Live Art Festival 2026.

blocks.caption: Official Poster for the ICA Live Art Festival 2026.

blocks.text: Suzette Bell-Roberts: The festival has long worked beyond conventional galleries and theatres. What changes when live art enters streets, public spaces, and heritage sites, and becomes part of the city’s everyday movement?

When live art becomes part of the city’s everyday movement, it makes the intricacies hidden in the rhythms of everyday life perceptible and engages directly with people and how they relate to various parts of the city. The city of Cape Town – loved for its vibrance – bears difficult histories that haunt the city. Live art activates these kinds of contradictions, connecting narratives across time. Collectively walking and experiencing live activations in the city enriches the way we understand it. Image of performance from ICA Live Art Festival 2023. Image courtesy from ICA.

blocks.caption: Image of performance from ICA Live Art Festival 2023. Image courtesy from ICA.

blocks.text: Cape Town remains profoundly shaped by an apartheid spatial geography, with many communities still separated from the city’s established cultural and economic centres. How does this history inform the festival’s decision to work across different parts of the city?

It’s central to our decision and remains one of the ICA’s main concerns. Apartheid spatial geography is a living violence. It limits access to the most basic components of livelihood and liveliness. It limits people’s shared experiences across different parts of the city. It limits freedom of mobility and encumbers meaningful solidarity. We hope that we can contribute to continuing efforts towards multidirectional mobility freedom, create moments for unexpected encounters and convergences, and to have presence in the many existing cultural hubs in Cape Town beyond the CBD.

This year the programme extends into KwaLanga for the first time through partnerships with 16 on Lerotholi and Guga S’Thebe. Why was it important to move beyond the city centre, and what does that shift make possible?

We are excited to be working with 16 on Lerotholi and Guga S’Thebe. 16 on Lerotholi is an incredible platform for the arts and we have deep respect for its founders. It was important for the Live Art festival to move beyond the city centre to forge networks across the city. We recognise that the concentration of cultural institutions in the CBD reinforces imbalances. Most galleries are in the city centre, even though the creative thinking is beyond the city centre. It illuminates the ways in which knowledge circulates. Image of performance from ICA Live Art Festival 2024. Image courtesy from ICA.

blocks.caption: Image of performance from ICA Live Art Festival 2024. Image courtesy from ICA.

blocks.text: The festival is free and open to all. What does meaningful cultural access mean to you, particularly for people who may have had little previous engagement with contemporary or live art?

This is very important to us. This is the kind of festival that should be accessible to everyone and encourage people to engage with the arts. We recognise that the value of creative work is not always monetary. Ours is to try and make it possible for all, regardless of financial means, to enjoy and participate in the arts.
What interests you about audiences who may encounter a work without having deliberately chosen to attend an art event, and how does that change the relationship between artist and public?

Knowledge is produced in the most unexpected places and through unexpected connections. Live art shifts the observer-observed relationship between the public and the artist. In some of the productions, the public can be more than just passive observers (unless, of course, they choose to be). Besides observing, they can participate, co-think, and converse. It is not just a relationship between the artist and the public but also among people interacting. We’re interested in catalysing those moments through incidental encounters between people who intentionally attend and those who serendipitously find and join us. Image of performance from ICA Live Art Festival 2024. Image courtesy from ICA.

blocks.caption: Image of performance from ICA Live Art Festival 2024. Image courtesy from ICA.

blocks.text: Cape Town’s public spaces carry very different histories depending on where one is in the city. How do those histories shape curatorial thinking around site, movement, and performance?

Cape Town’s histories are key to the curatorial process. Histories of enslavement, imperialism, spatial segregation and dispossession overshadow the city and shape today’s social interactions. The curatorial team remained sensitive to this. We approached this festival through an open call and some of the proposals were site-specific, addressing specific histories embedded in place, while others capture the human habits cultivated through those histories. Other works activate the city in various ways by juxtaposing different histories in a given site.

There is a difference between taking a festival into another part of the city and developing a programme that is genuinely shaped by that place. How has the KwaLanga context influenced the festival rather than simply serving as a new venue?

KwaLanga connects histories with it as part of the city (keeping in mind histories of extraction). We start the route from Mendi Avenue to the Beer Hall, 16 on Lerotholi, and Guga S’Thebe, artists revive 20th-century labour histories to show the current impact. We also recognise KwaLanga’s ingenuity in transfiguring those histories. Image of performance from ICA Live Art Festival 2024. Image courtesy from ICA.

blocks.caption: Image of performance from ICA Live Art Festival 2024. Image courtesy from ICA.

blocks.text: Looking at this edition as a whole, what becomes possible when contemporary art is less concentrated in the places where established art audiences already know to look for it?
What becomes possible are fresh perspectives, a rethinking of positionalities and an immediacy between art and the city (art does not merely reflect what is happening but shapes it).

The ICA Live Art Festival 2026 takes place from 14 to 18 October 2026 across Cape Town’s streets, squares, heritage sites, and cultural spaces in the CBD, UCT, and KwaLanga. On Sunday, 18 October, the festival moves through KwaLanga, beginning on Mendi Avenue, continuing to 16 Lerotholi, and concluding at Guga S’Thebe.
